sections.title: Metabolic Management: Gyrate Atrophy Focus
content: Cataract surgery: Primary surgical intervention.
Arginine restricted diet to decrease ornithine levels.
Vit B6 supplementation to reduce plasma ornithine.
Clinical Pearl: Gyrate atrophy is caused by OAT gene mutations; Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is a cofactor for the OAT enzyme.

branches: Kinest Dysplasia: High myopia, ectopia lentis, vitreous degeneration, RD, short stature, round face, arthropathy

rows: Empty vitreous, Retrolental membrane, Circumferential equatorial membranes extending into vitreous cavity.
Radial lattice degeneration with RPE hyperplasia, Vascular sheathing, Sclerosis.
Retinal detachment (50% in 1st decade), Multiple giant tears (bilateral).
Mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, Early onset osteoarthritis.
Presenile cataract (peripheral cortical wedge shaped, fleck or lamellar opacities).
Glaucoma associated with congenital angle anomaly.
Pierre Robin Sequence: Glossoptosis, micrognathia, and cleft palate often cluster.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Cherry Red Spot at Macula

rows: CRAO, cilioretinal artery occlusion, Commotio retinae
GM1 gangliosidosis, Mucolipidosis type 1 (sialidosis), GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff), Niemann-Pick disease, Faber disease
Quinine, Dapsone, Gentamycin, CO poisoning, Methanol toxicity

sections.title: Risk Factors for Progression to Detachment
content: 1. History of RD in the fellow eye
2. Prior cataract surgery + vitreous loss
3. Myopia
4. +ve family history of RD
5. Systemic condition (Marfan, Stickler, Ehlers Danlos syndromes)
6. Symptomatic breaks associated with an acute PVD
7. Large breaks
8. Persistent vitreoretinal traction
9. U-shaped tears
10. Superior breaks (superotemporal), equatorial breaks
11. Aphakic (rare)

sections.title: Clinical Settings & RD Chronicity
content: Laser Retinopexy: Spot size 200-300 (3-mirror) or 100-200 (wide field); Power 200mW; Duration 0.1sec.
Signs of Long-standing RD: Retinal thinning, Intraretinal cysts (1 year), Subretinal demarcation lines (3 months).
Clinical Pearl: Demarcation lines indicate the RPE's attempt to 'self-wall off' the detachment.

branches: Secondary: RD or Idiopathic Uveal Effusion Syndrome

sections.title: Uveal Effusion Syndrome Details
sections.content: Idiopathic, bilateral condition typically in middle-aged hypermetropic men. Often associated with nanophthalmos. Cause: Impairment of fluid drainage via abnormal thickened sclera or vortex veins. Signs: Mild/absent inflammation, cilioretinal detachment followed by exudative RD. Post-resolution: RPE shows leopard spot mottling due to high protein concentration in SRF. DD: Secondary uveal effusion, choroidal hemorrhage, ring melanoma. Treatment: Full thickness sclerectomy in nanophthalmos.

sections.title: Scleral Buckle: Technique & Complications
content: Technique: Periotomy -> Localization -> Cryotherapy -> Explant sutured -> SRF Drainage.
Complications: Diplopia, CMO (25%), ERM (15%), Anterior segment ischaemia.
Buckle Issues: Extrusion, intrusion, infection, elevated IOP/angle closure.
Failure Causes: Missed break, Fish-mouthing (large superior equatorial tear opening widely), PVR (late failure), Buckle height decrease.

sections.title: Exudative Retinal Detachment Causes
content: 1. Choroidal tumour (Melanoma, haemangioma, metastasis)
2. Inflammation (Harada disease, posterior scleritis)
3. Bullous CSR (rare)
4. Iatrogenic (RD surgery, PRP)
5. Choroidal neovascularization
6. Hypertensive choroidopathy (toxaemia of pregnancy)
7. Idiopathic (choroidal effusion syndrome)

sections.title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: Indications: Masked breaks (VH, debris, PCO, IOL edge), Giant tears, PVR, Tractional RD (foveal), Combined TRD/RRD, Penetrating trauma.
Intraoperative Complications: Posterior/Peripheral retinal breaks, Choroidal haemorrhage.

Postoperative Complications: RRD, Retinal folds, Inflammation (diabetics), Raised IOP (gas expansion, oil glaucoma, ghost cell, steroid-induced), Cataract (feathering/nucleosclerosis), Band keratopathy.
Pneumatic Retinopexy Indications: Uncomplicated RD with small breaks, clusters < 2 clock hours in upper 2/3 of retina.

sections.title: Vitreous Haemorrhage Etiology
content: Acute PVD
Proliferative retinopathy (DM, RVO, Sickle cell, Eales disease, Vasculitis)
Macroaneurysm, Telangiectasia, Capillary haemangioma
Trauma
Systemic bleeding disorder, Terson syndrome

sections.title: Motility: Basic Measurements
sections.content: Near Point of Convergence (NPC): The nearest point on which the eye can maintain binocular fixation (normally nearer than 10cm without undue effort). Near Point of Accommodation (NPA): The nearest point on which the eyes can maintain clear focus.

sections.title: Brown Syndrome: Classification & Care
content: Mild: No hypotropia in primary position; No downshoot in adduction.
Moderate: No hypotropia in primary position; Downshoot in adduction.
Severe: Hypotropia in primary position; Downshoot in adduction; Chin-up head posture.
Congenital Treatment: Observation if binocular function holds. Indications for surgery: Primary hypotropia or head posture. Procedure: Lengthening of Superior Oblique (SO) tendon.
Acquired Treatment: Steroids (oral or injection near trochlea).

sections.title: Differential: Brown Syndrome vs. Inferior Oblique (IO) Palsy
V-Pattern & A-Pattern Strabismus
sections.content: V-Pattern: Significant if difference between upgaze and downgaze >= 15 prism. Causes: IOOA with 4th nerve palsy, SO underaction + IOOA (infantile ET), SR underaction, Brown syndrome, Craniofacial anomalies. Treatment: Oblique weakening/strengthening. If no oblique dysfunction: Bilateral MR recession with downward transposition or LR recession with upward transposition. A-Pattern: Significant if difference >= 10 prism. Face turn away from affected eye. Causes: Primary SO overaction (Exo in primary), IO underaction, IR underaction. Treatment: SO posterior tenotomy (corrects 20PD) or total tenotomy (50PD). If no oblique dysfunction: Bilateral MR recession with upward transposition (ET) or LR recession with downward transposition (XT).

sections.title: Strabismus Surgery: Complications & Botox
content: Operative Risks: Lost/slipped muscle (Medial Rectus), Globe perforation (High myopia), Posterior Tenon capsule opening (fibrosis/fat involvement).
Postoperative Risks: Over/under correction, Anterior segment ischaemia, Stretched scar (years later).

Botulinum Toxin Indications: Small angle residual squint, Infantile esotropia, Active thyroid orbitopathy, Determining diplopia risk, Assessing BSV potential, Lateral rectus palsy, Psychosocial unacceptable deviation after multiple surgeries.
